difficultyReason: EXCEPT format. The argument involves a multi-step policy chain (legible labeling → informed consumer choice → healthier diets). Four answers strengthen distinct links; one (the correct answer) appears supportive on the surface but actually addresses a neighboring claim rather than the argument's conclusion.
stimulus: A consumer advocacy group argues that requiring restaurants to display calorie counts prominently on menus will improve public health outcomes. Diners who see calorie information, the group contends, will make lower-calorie choices, and consistently lower-calorie choices lead to reduced rates of diet-related illness. The group therefore urges all municipalities to mandate prominent calorie labeling on restaurant menus.
questionStem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the consumer advocacy group's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: In cities where calorie labeling was mandated, average per-meal calorie consumption at restaurants decreased significantly within two years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who habitually consume fewer calories than the average for their demographic group have lower rates of diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys show that the majority of diners report that they would choose lower-calorie options if calorie information were clearly available at the point of ordering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restaurants that voluntarily adopted calorie labeling before any mandate reported an increase in overall customer satisfaction scores.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Longitudinal studies indicate that sustained reductions in daily caloric intake correlate strongly with decreased incidence of diet-related chronic illnesses.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion is that mandatory calorie labeling will improve public health. Customer satisfaction is entirely disconnected from the health-outcome chain the argument traces. D neither rules out an alternative explanation nor confirms a load-bearing premise linking labeling to healthier choices to better health. It is therefore the one answer that does NOT strengthen the argument.
explanations.A: Strengthens — directly confirms that labeling causes lower-calorie choices, a key causal link in the argument.
explanations.B: Strengthens — supports the premise that lower-calorie choices reduce diet-related illness.
explanations.C: Strengthens — supports the premise that diners will act on calorie information when displayed.
explanations.D: Correct (does not strengthen). Customer satisfaction scores are irrelevant to the health-improvement conclusion.
explanations.E: Strengthens — bolsters the premise that sustained caloric reduction leads to fewer chronic illnesses.

difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain in medicine. The correct answer addresses a non-obvious implicit assumption — that the observed biomarker reduction actually reflects the proposed mechanism rather than a confounding drug interaction. Distractors include a plausible-sounding choice that strengthens only a neighboring claim.
stimulus: Researchers studying patients with chronic inflammatory arthritis found that those who began taking a new omega-3 supplement showed a marked reduction in serum levels of interleukin-6, a key inflammatory marker, after twelve weeks. The researchers concluded that omega-3 supplementation directly suppresses interleukin-6 production in joint tissue, thereby reducing inflammation.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Interleukin-6 is known to be a reliable indicator of systemic inflammation in patients with chronic arthritis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: None of the patients in the study changed their dosage of anti-inflammatory medications during the twelve-week supplementation period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other omega-3 supplements produced by different manufacturers have also been shown to reduce inflammatory symptoms in arthritis patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patients who showed the greatest reduction in interleukin-6 also reported the most significant improvements in joint mobility.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Omega-3 fatty acids have been used as dietary supplements for purposes unrelated to inflammation for several decades.

explanations.correct: The researchers attribute the IL-6 reduction to the omega-3 supplement specifically. A rival explanation is that changes in patients' anti-inflammatory medication drove the reduction. B rules out that alternative by confirming medication dosages were unchanged, directly strengthening the causal attribution to omega-3.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — confirming IL-6 is a reliable marker doesn't establish that omega-3 caused its reduction.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out confounding medication changes as an alternative explanation for the observed reduction.
explanations.C: Strengthens a broader claim about omega-3 supplements generally, not the specific mechanistic conclusion about this supplement suppressing IL-6 in joint tissue.
explanations.D: Shows a correlation between IL-6 reduction and symptom improvement but does not address whether omega-3 caused the IL-6 reduction in the first place.
explanations.E: Irrelevant — longevity of use for other purposes says nothing about the causal mechanism proposed.

difficultyReason: Analogical argument in law/economics. The correct answer closes an analogical gap by establishing that the key structural feature making the analogy work actually holds in the target case. Distractors include a surface-plausible choice that strengthens the source case rather than the analogy.
stimulus: A legal scholar argues that recent antitrust rulings against dominant social media platforms should be modeled on the landmark breakup of telecommunications monopolies in the 1980s. In that case, breaking up a single dominant provider spurred innovation, lowered consumer prices, and created a more competitive market. The scholar concludes that applying similar remedies to dominant social media companies would produce comparable benefits.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the legal scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The telecommunications breakup of the 1980s is widely regarded by economists as one of the most successful antitrust interventions in American history.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Social media platforms, like telecommunications providers in the 1980s, derive their dominance primarily from network effects and control of essential infrastructure rather than from superior products alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several technology companies that emerged after previous antitrust actions in the software industry went on to become dominant platforms themselves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Consumer advocacy groups in multiple countries have called for stricter regulation of social media companies' data practices.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The federal agencies responsible for antitrust enforcement currently have more resources than they did during the telecommunications case.

explanations.correct: The scholar's analogy depends on social media platforms sharing the structural features that made the telecom breakup effective (network effects, infrastructure control). B confirms that the same dominance-conferring mechanism applies in both cases, directly closing the analogical gap and strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.A: Strengthens only the source side of the analogy — it confirms the telecom precedent was successful, but does not establish that social media platforms are relevantly similar.
explanations.B: Correct. Establishes the shared structural feature (network effects + infrastructure control) that underpins the analogy's validity.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative outcome (new dominant companies emerging post-breakup) that if anything raises doubt about the effectiveness of the remedy — a mild weakener.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — advocacy group calls for data regulation address a different issue than the structural antitrust argument.
explanations.E: Addresses enforcement capacity, not the structural similarity that makes the analogy work.

difficultyReason: Environmental science causal argument with a non-obvious load-bearing assumption. The correct answer confirms a mechanism (bioaccumulation pathway) that is implicit but necessary for the conclusion. A strong distractor rules out a different alternative cause, making it appear equally valid.
stimulus: Ecologists monitoring a coastal estuary found that osprey populations declined sharply following the expansion of a nearby agricultural operation. They noted elevated concentrations of organophosphate pesticides in estuary fish — the osprey's primary food source. The ecologists concluded that pesticide bioaccumulation through the food chain is responsible for the osprey population decline.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No new residential development occurred near the estuary in the three years preceding the osprey population decline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Osprey populations in estuaries without elevated pesticide concentrations in local fish remained stable over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Organophosphate pesticides at concentrations found in the estuary fish have been shown in laboratory studies to impair osprey reproductive success and juvenile survival rates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The agricultural operation expanded its pesticide use by more than 40 percent in the two years before the osprey decline was first recorded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several other bird species in the estuary region also experienced population declines during the same period.

explanations.correct: The argument needs a mechanism linking pesticide concentrations in fish to actual osprey population decline. C confirms that the specific pesticide levels observed are sufficient to harm osprey reproduction and survival — the non-obvious biological link that makes the causal chain complete.
explanations.A: Rules out habitat disruption from residential development, which is a legitimate alternative cause to eliminate, but this is a weaker strengthener than C because it doesn't confirm the proposed mechanism — it only rules out one of many possible alternatives.
explanations.B: Provides correlational support but functions more as an epidemiological comparison than a mechanistic confirmation; it doesn't establish that the pesticides specifically caused the decline.
explanations.C: Correct. Confirms the operative biological mechanism at the observed concentration levels, directly supporting the causal conclusion.
explanations.D: Establishes a temporal correlation between expanded pesticide use and the decline, but temporal correlation alone doesn't confirm bioaccumulation as the mechanism.
explanations.E: Could indicate a broader environmental stressor affecting multiple species, which might actually weaken the argument by suggesting a different common cause.

difficultyReason: EXCEPT format in technology/ethics domain. The argument involves a data privacy policy conclusion reached via a rights-based and consequentialist chain. Four answers strengthen distinct premises; the correct non-strengthener sounds ethically relevant but addresses a claim the argument never makes.
stimulus: A technology ethicist argues that social networking companies should be legally prohibited from selling users' personal data to third-party advertisers without explicit, opt-in consent. Users have a right to control information about themselves, and allowing companies to profit from that information without meaningful consent treats users as commodities rather than autonomous agents. Moreover, unsolicited targeted advertising has been shown to cause measurable psychological distress in frequent social media users.
questionStem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the ethicist's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The majority of social media users are unaware that their personal data is routinely sold to third-party advertisers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studies conducted across multiple countries found that targeted advertising exposure correlates with increased rates of anxiety and compulsive consumption behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When given a clear opt-in choice regarding data sharing, most users in pilot programs chose not to allow their data to be sold to advertisers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Social networking companies that adopted opt-in consent policies reported no significant decline in total advertising revenue after implementation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Third-party advertisers that purchase personal data often share it with additional entities without informing either the original platform or the user.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's argument is grounded in users' rights and the psychological harms of unsolicited targeting — not in whether opt-in policies harm companies financially. D addresses a business-impact concern the argument never raises, so it neither confirms a premise nor rules out an alternative. It does not strengthen the rights-based or harm-based reasoning, making it the one answer that fails to strengthen.
explanations.A: Strengthens — lack of awareness undermines the claim that current consent is meaningful, supporting the need for explicit opt-in requirements.
explanations.B: Strengthens — directly supports the psychological distress premise central to the argument.
explanations.C: Strengthens — shows users would exercise the right to refuse if given genuine opt-in choice, supporting the autonomy premise.
explanations.D: Correct (does not strengthen). Revenue impact on companies is irrelevant to the argument's rights-based and harm-based foundations.
explanations.E: Strengthens — compounds the harm and lack of control users experience, reinforcing both the autonomy and distress premises.

difficultyReason: Historical causal argument with a non-obvious implicit assumption. The correct answer supports an unstated premise about the causal direction of the relationship. A prominent distractor introduces an alternative explanation that students might mistake for the argument's support.
stimulus: Historians studying the decline of artisan guilds in 16th-century northern Europe have noted that guild membership dropped precipitously in cities where municipal governments began issuing direct licenses to individual craftsmen. The historians argue that this licensing policy undermined the guilds' monopoly on legitimate trade and therefore caused their decline.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historians' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cities that issued direct craftsman licenses also tended to experience rapid population growth during the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In cities where municipal licensing was introduced, guild membership began declining within a decade of the policy's adoption, whereas guild membership remained stable in comparable cities without such policies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many artisans who left guilds after municipal licensing was introduced went on to establish successful independent workshops.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some northern European guilds had already been experiencing internal governance disputes before municipal licensing policies were adopted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The craft goods produced by guild members were generally of higher quality than those produced by independently licensed artisans.

explanations.correct: The historians need to establish that licensing policy — rather than some other factor — caused the guild decline. B provides a controlled comparison: cities with licensing saw decline; comparable cities without licensing did not. This rules out general historical trends as the cause and confirms the causal role of the policy, directly strengthening the argument.
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative explanation — rapid population growth may have disrupted guilds independently of licensing, making this a potential weakener or at best irrelevant.
explanations.B: Correct. The controlled comparison between licensing and non-licensing cities isolates the policy as the causal factor, ruling out coincidental historical trends.
explanations.C: Shows a consequence of leaving guilds but does not address whether licensing caused the leaving — it could even suggest the choice was voluntary and not driven by the policy's coercive effect.
explanations.D: Introduces an internal alternative cause (governance disputes) that pre-dates the licensing policy — this potentially weakens the historians' causal claim.
explanations.E: Addresses quality differences but is irrelevant to whether licensing policy caused guild decline.

difficultyReason: Economics predictive argument. The correct answer confirms an implicit structural assumption. A strong distractor strengthens a neighboring empirical claim rather than the predictive conclusion about future market behavior. Another distractor introduces a new variable that sounds relevant but is actually a rival causal factor.
stimulus: An economist predicts that the recent surge in remote work will permanently reduce commercial office vacancy rates in city centers, as companies downsize their leased office space. She cites surveys showing that most large corporations plan to reduce their office footprints by at least 20 percent over the next five years. Therefore, she concludes, urban commercial real estate prices will decline substantially in the coming decade.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Remote work arrangements have been shown to increase employee productivity in a wide range of industries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Municipal governments in several large cities have already begun converting vacant office buildings to residential use, indicating awareness of a coming supply imbalance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commercial real estate prices in city centers have historically declined when vacancy rates exceed a threshold significantly lower than current projections.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A number of large corporations that reduced office space during previous economic downturns subsequently expanded their footprints when conditions improved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Survey respondents from the technology sector were disproportionately represented in the data showing planned office footprint reductions.

explanations.correct: The economist's argument runs: remote work → corporate office downsizing → higher vacancy rates → lower commercial real estate prices. The weakest implicit link is whether increased vacancy will actually translate into price declines. C confirms that historical vacancy–price relationships operate at thresholds consistent with current projections, directly supporting the final predictive step.
explanations.A: Supports the premise that remote work is sustainable, but the economist already accepts that; it doesn't advance the vacancy-to-price-decline conclusion.
explanations.B: Indicates awareness of a supply problem but could actually weaken the argument — if conversions absorb excess supply, prices might not fall as much.
explanations.C: Correct. Confirms the historical mechanism by which the projected vacancy levels cause price declines, supporting the argument's pivotal final inference.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative historical pattern — corporate re-expansion — that actually undermines the prediction of permanent downsizing.
explanations.E: Raises a methodological concern about survey representativeness that potentially weakens the corporate-downsizing premise.

difficultyReason: Linguistics causal argument with a subtle alternative-explanation trap. The correct answer rules out the most plausible rival explanation, but identifying that rival requires understanding the argument's implicit structure. A distractor appears to rule out an alternative but actually addresses an irrelevant variable.
stimulus: Linguists studying a remote community found that children raised in households where two distinct languages were spoken with equal frequency developed larger working-memory capacities than monolingual children in the same community. The linguists argued that the constant task of managing two competing linguistic systems exercises executive function, thereby expanding working-memory capacity.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguists' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bilingual and monolingual households in the study were matched for parental education levels and household income.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two languages spoken in the bilingual households belonged to different language families and shared virtually no grammatical structures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Working-memory capacity has been linked by numerous studies to academic achievement in mathematics and reading comprehension.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Children in the study community who attended bilingual schools showed the same working-memory advantage as those raised in bilingual homes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Monolingual children in the community had the same access to educational resources, nutrition, and healthcare as the bilingual children.

explanations.correct: The most plausible alternative explanation for the working-memory difference is socioeconomic or educational factors: bilingual households might systematically differ in parental education or income, which independently predict cognitive development. A rules out that rival by confirming the groups were matched on these variables, strengthening the causal attribution to bilingualism itself.
explanations.A: Correct. Rules out the key socioeconomic confound — parental education and income — that would otherwise explain the working-memory difference without invoking bilingualism.
explanations.B: Addresses linguistic distance between the two languages but does not rule out a confound or confirm the mechanism — it is irrelevant to why bilingual children have larger working memories.
explanations.C: Establishes working memory's importance generally but does not address the causal claim about bilingualism producing working-memory gains.
explanations.D: Extends the finding to a different setting but still doesn't isolate bilingualism as the cause versus other features of bilingual school environments.
explanations.E: Rules out healthcare and nutrition differences, which are less plausible confounds than socioeconomic status; answer A addresses the more directly relevant and well-established confound.

difficultyReason: Arts/cultural policy argument. Requires recognizing which answer bridges the argument's implicit assumption that a particular policy instrument will achieve its intended cultural effect. The strongest distractor strengthens the desirability of the goal rather than the efficacy of the means.
stimulus: A cultural policy analyst contends that public subsidies for regional theater companies increase the overall artistic diversity of a nation's cultural landscape. Without such subsidies, only commercially viable productions would survive, leading to the homogenization of theatrical repertoire. The analyst concludes that governments should maintain or expand public funding for regional theater.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surveys consistently show that citizens place high value on having access to a diverse range of cultural and artistic experiences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In countries where public theater subsidies were reduced or eliminated, the number of productions featuring experimental, non-commercial, or minority-language works declined sharply.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regional theater companies that receive public subsidies employ significantly more local artists than do commercially funded productions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Private philanthropic funding for the arts has increased in several countries that reduced public theater subsidies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The administrative costs of distributing public theater subsidies represent a small fraction of overall national arts budgets.

explanations.correct: The analyst's conclusion depends on the empirical claim that removing subsidies causes repertoire homogenization. B provides direct historical evidence confirming exactly this mechanism — in places where subsidies were cut, diverse and non-commercial works declined. This confirms both that subsidies sustain diversity and that their removal causes homogenization, directly supporting the policy conclusion.
explanations.A: Strengthens the value of the goal (diverse culture is desired) but not the claim that subsidies are the necessary or effective means to achieve it.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms the causal mechanism: subsidy reduction → decline in non-commercial works → homogenization. Directly supports the argument's central causal premise.
explanations.C: Supports a different benefit of subsidies (local employment) rather than the diversity argument the analyst makes.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative funding mechanism that could replace subsidies — this potentially weakens the argument by suggesting subsidies are not necessary for sustaining diverse theater.
explanations.E: Addresses cost-efficiency, which is a separate consideration from whether subsidies actually achieve diversity — irrelevant to the argument's conclusion.

difficultyReason: EXCEPT format in environmental science/policy with a multi-premise argument. Four answers strengthen different links in the causal-normative chain. The correct non-strengthener addresses an empirical claim that is not part of the argument's logic but sounds topically relevant, making it a classic 'strengthens a different conclusion' trap.
stimulus: An environmental scientist argues that urban green corridors — continuous strips of vegetation linking city parks — should be prioritized in municipal planning because they enable wildlife to move safely between habitat patches. Isolated habitat patches lead to local species extinctions due to inbreeding and resource depletion, while connected corridors allow for genetic exchange and resource replenishment. The scientist concludes that cities without green corridors will inevitably experience greater urban biodiversity loss than cities that establish them.
questionStem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the environmental scientist's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban wildlife populations in cities with established green corridors show significantly greater genetic diversity than populations in cities of similar size without such corridors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Species that are unable to disperse between isolated urban habitat patches have been documented going locally extinct at higher rates than species capable of moving across larger ranges.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Computer models of habitat connectivity consistently predict that adding corridor vegetation between isolated patches reduces extinction probability for resident species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Green corridors in urban areas also reduce the urban heat island effect by increasing vegetative cover, lowering ambient temperatures in surrounding neighborhoods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cities that have invested in green corridors report that wildlife monitoring programs in those corridors detect species previously absent from the urban core.

explanations.correct: The scientist's argument is specifically about green corridors preventing biodiversity loss through wildlife movement and genetic exchange. D identifies a genuine benefit of green corridors — urban heat reduction — but that benefit is entirely outside the argument's logical chain. It neither supports the movement-enables-genetic-exchange premise nor connects to the biodiversity-loss conclusion. It strengthens a different conclusion (green corridors benefit cities via temperature reduction), not the one the scientist actually argues.
explanations.A: Strengthens — directly confirms that corridors produce the genetic diversity benefit the argument predicts.
explanations.B: Strengthens — confirms the premise that isolation causes local extinction due to inability to disperse.
explanations.C: Strengthens — provides modeling evidence that corridors reduce extinction probability, supporting the conclusion.
explanations.D: Correct (does not strengthen). The heat island benefit is real but irrelevant to the biodiversity-loss argument.
explanations.E: Strengthens — confirms corridors enable wildlife movement and recolonization, directly supporting the connectivity premise.
